rows.en:
This time, the one running for their life wasn't a high school girl.
It was a man... a police officer.
It was a scene of a police officer running for his life.
"This is strange. It's not what I saw yesterday."
And then the officer was killed, just like the high school girl the day before.
"A different tape...?"
That couldn't be.
"Maybe there are several scenes recorded on it..."
He checked the tape and rewound it, but it began with the same police officer scene.
And after that, there was nothing on it at all.{p}

He checked every video in his room, but the tape of the high school girl being killed was nowhere to be found.
Tokita went to the school at the same hour the officer had been killed on the tape.{p}

In the schoolyard, ropes had been strung up around the spot where the high school girl was killed.
There was no body where the officer had been killed in the video.
"Looks like it hasn't happened yet."
He was certain that a police officer was going to be killed.
And so Tokita waited.
He waited a long time.
But everything around him was hushed and still.
Now and then, a patrol car drove past.
"If I keep hanging around like this, they'll get suspicious of me."
It was just as he was about to head home.{p}

"Gyaaaah!"
It was a man's scream.
Tokita stared at the sight as if he were watching a scene from a movie.
I suppose he could no longer tell reality from the movies.{p}

From that day on, every night, he chased down the scenes recorded on the videotape.
Tokita no longer needed to ask his friends to record movies for him.{p}

"Hey, Tokita, you've stopped asking us to tape stuff for you lately."
"I found something much more interesting."
That's the kind of thing he said.
Then, one day, it happened.{p}

After school, he went home and watched the video, as always.
"I wonder what kind of scene it'll be today."{p}

The footage showed the school at night.
But suddenly, the picture went fuzzy and stopped.{p}

"Huh, that's weird... Well, as long as I know where it is."
With that in mind, he headed for the school that night.{p}

"It should be around here..."
Some time passed, but nothing happened.
"That's strange. Maybe nothing's happening today..."
And then, just as he turned around to go home...{p}

And then he died.
Hm? How do I know this story?
The truth is, that day I'd gone to his house to get back a tape I'd lent him earlier.
He wasn't home, but his mother showed me to his room and let me check his tapes.
And I saw it. Footage of him being killed.
At the time, just like him, I thought it was some amateur film or something and didn't think much of it.
But when night came, I couldn't get it out of my mind, so I went to the school to see.
And sure enough, it had already happened.
I don't know what became of that video afterward.
I wonder whose murder will show up on it next.
That's the end of my story.
Next person, please.{p}

I see.
So you like action?
You can really tell that action movies these days keep getting more and more extreme and intense.
And a lot of them are very well made, too.
But I don't care much for action movies myself.
You see, action movies are nearly always full of stunt people, aren't they?
I can't bear to watch them.
I feel so sorry for them that I can't enjoy the movie.
I find myself wondering whether that stuntman was badly injured afterward, and so on.
I'm timid, you see.
I tend to imagine what goes on on the filmmakers' side.
Because in my first year, there was someone in my class who made movies.
Amateur films, mind you.{p}

His name was Yasuo Tokita.
He truly loved movies.
He was so sad our school had no film club that he went as far as rounding people up and forming an unofficial one himself.
The truth is, Tokita wanted desperately to be an actor.
He once told me it was his dream for the future.
Apparently he idolized Bruce Lee.
I heard he'd been learning martial arts under his father's instruction.
Tokita was also the director of the club.
I suppose he wanted to direct his own films and act in them, too.
In the lead role, of course.{p}

After all, Tokita founded the club, and he was the one who brought in the equipment.
So the senior members gladly agreed to let him be both director and star.
And so filming began on the club's memorable first production.
I think it was right around this time last year.
The genre he chose to shoot was action, of course.
If I remember right, the title of the movie was
"Fist of Justice☆"
I think that was it.
Oh dear, it makes me laugh somehow.
The plot went roughly like this.
The hero's father was a famous martial artist.
One day, he was hired as a bodyguard by a certain organization.
He learned the organization's secret, and he was killed for it.
The premise was that his son, the hero, takes on the organization to avenge his father.{p}

Well, it was a student club, after all.
Most of it was set inside the school or in the schoolyard.
The hero and his father were both played by students.
Quite a dubious father and son, weren't they?
Even so, somehow or other, they finished shooting.{p}

"...Huh?
That's weird.
Did we shoot a scene like this?"
Tokita looked at one of the reels and tilted his head, puzzled.{p}

It showed the hero teaching martial arts forms to the young students of his dojo.
They had shot a scene like that, but this was different from what he remembered.
Tokita was astonished when he watched the film.
Everyone, whose acting had been so clumsy, was as good as real actors.
Everyone moved swiftly, exactly as he instructed them.
It was almost enough to fool him into thinking his teaching really was that good and they were all improving by leaps and bounds.
That's how well it had been shot.{p}

He didn't remember shooting a cut like that.
But maybe he was misremembering.
There was no way Tokita would leave out a scene that good.
He edited that scene in.{p}

But the next day, while watching another reel, he found yet another scene he didn't remember shooting.
It was the scene where the hero's father learns the organization's secret and is killed.
The death scene they had actually shot was a simple one.
He runs, chased by a hitman the organization has hired.
The hitman closes in behind him.
Then, his scream.
The hitman walks away, his back to the dead man.
And yet, that film clearly showed him dying.
And how real it was!
The hitman's iron fist explodes into his stomach.
Perhaps because it caught him square in the solar plexus, a thin line of bright red blood ran from his mouth...
Then he falls to the ground and stops moving.
One cut like that after another appeared on the screen.{p}
It was the very next day.

The student who played the hero's father was killed.
It was Katayama, who was in the same year as Tokita and me.
He'd been punched in the stomach over and over.
Hard enough to rupture his internal organs, I heard.
When Tokita heard how it had happened, he couldn't believe his ears.
It was exactly like that scene, wasn't it?
Apparently they never found out who beat him to death.
After all, he'd been sleeping alone in his own room in the middle of the night.
There was no sign that anyone had snuck in, and the room didn't look disturbed.
Naturally, the family would be the ones suspected.
Tokita became terrified.{p}

What if Katayama had died because Tokita had edited that film...?
What if this was the curse of that film...?
What would you think, if it were you?
Would you want to keep on editing that movie?{p}Because if you kept going, something even stranger might show up on it.
Keep editing
Stop now

Heh heh... You're cruel, aren't you?
With a personality like that, I won't answer for what happens to you.
But Tokita was the same.
He loved movies to death, after all.
This movie might just go down in history as a masterpiece.{p}

The hero, looking cool, beating assassin after assassin to death.
The assassins, dying more realistically than ever.
Tokita was in a great mood by now.
Every time he saw the hero take down another assassin, he pumped his fist too.
And then came the scene where the hero defeats the final boss.
The instant the hero's finishing punch was about to explode into the boss's stomach...
The boss dodged the hero's fist and threw a punch of his own.
Tokita couldn't believe his eyes.{p}

"No way...
This is wrong!"
If you ask me, it could never have been shot that well in the first place, so that itself was what was wrong.
Tokita thought he might have seen it wrong, and tried to watch it again.{p}Would you watch it again, {a}?
Watch it again
Don't watch it
Tokita, too, decided to watch the movie again, and rewound the film.{p}

Then the scene in question came up.
He stared at it, his eyes wide as saucers.
The hero's punch was about to land... or so it seemed.
"Not again★"
The hero's punch only grazed the air.
The boss's punch slammed into the hero...{p}
At that moment, the boss's punch burst out of the screen and caught Tokita square in the face.{p}

"Bguh!"
He let out a short grunt.
In rapid succession, lightning-fast punches struck his face and upper body.
His face twisted as if its bones were broken, and blood came gushing and gurgling out of his mouth.{p}

Blood got in his eyes, and everything looked as if it were covered in red cellophane.
Beyond it, Tokita saw it clearly.
Katayama, leaning out of the screen and laughing...
That face wasn't the face of the student who played the boss. It was Katayama's.
Tokita died from the shock of the beating and his ruptured internal organs.{p}

Despite the police investigation, the case went unsolved, I hear.
You're asking how I know all this?{p}

One day, I found a box with film in it inside my desk at school.
I held the film up to the sunlight and looked at it.
I couldn't really make anything out that way, and I was intrigued, so I went out of my way to buy an 8mm projector to watch it.
For some reason, I was gripped by an urge to see that film.{p}

I didn't have a screen, so I used the white wall of my room.
When I saw it, I was dumbstruck.
It was a complete record of everything leading up to his death.
And the film ended at the moment he was killed.{p}

"Uwaaaaaaaaargh!"
With my eyes shut tight, I quickly switched off the projector beside me.{p}

When I slowly raised my head, there was nothing there but my room, the same as always.
If I'd been a little slower switching it off, I might not be here now.
The film?
I burned it.
Yes, it burned very well.
Mixed in with the crackling of the burning film, I thought I heard Tokita screaming.
Was that just my imagination...?
Ever since then, I keep seeing his crushed face on the white wall of my room.
That's the end of my story.
We're finally at the last one, aren't we?
Now, next person... go ahead.{p}

Suspense, is it?
I see. I quite enjoy the feeling of tension myself.
Murder stories are especially good.
The hero, sensing danger, slowly being cornered by the killer...
I just love that kind of thrill.
Heh heh heh...
Well, let's save that subject for another time.
What I'll be telling you about this time has to do with a sci-fi movie.{p}

Did you know there was a film club at this school until a few months ago?
There was a student in that club named Tokita.
He loved sci-fi, and he was often reading sci-fi novels and magazines during breaks and such.
A mere school club can't make flashy sci-fi, after all.
Though real sci-fi isn't about depicting spaceships and future worlds with special effects anyway.{p}

The next day, the research team came.
Tokita watched them with great curiosity, too.
He loved this sort of thing, after all.
The investigation began with the school's students and teachers looking on.
The school treated it as part of their education and didn't impose any particular restrictions.
In the middle of all that, the sheet covering the stone was taken off.{p}

But the stone, which had been big and round when it was found, had split open.
Some said it was someone's nasty prank, but it was decided that the heat that had lasted since the day before was to blame, and the investigation went on.
And then that day's investigation was over.
After the team left, he went up to the stone.
It was made of perfectly ordinary rock.
"Huh, how boring."
I suppose he'd been hoping something would come out of the split stone.
But even looking at the stone's cross-section, there was no hollow inside, and Tokita's hopes were dashed.{p}

Just then, from the direction of the old school building, there came a sound like something giving off smoke.
You know how soda and such goes fizz?
It was like a much bigger version of that.
Something is there.
Tokita couldn't shake that feeling.
Could something have come out of the stone and be wandering around?
His hopes rising once again, he headed toward the old school building.{p}

When Tokita reached the front of the old school building, he looked around.
But there was nothing there that lived up to his hopes.
As he gave up and turned to go home, there it was again: a fizz... fizz... sound.
This time he could clearly tell it was coming from inside the old school building.
He crept quietly into the old school building.{p}

There, he found a small animal.
It was a creature like a chick, shining silver.
No bird like this exists on Earth.
Thinking about it, it should have been eerie, but to Tokita, it looked enchanting.
He decided to keep it in the old school building.{p}

Then he came up with the idea of using this animal to make a movie.
When he told the club members about it, they all agreed.
And so they started filming.
The story was a drama about the friendship between an alien creature and a human high school student.
Filming went smoothly.{p}

One day, the creature spun a cocoon and went inside it.
"Oh well.
We'll work around it in the editing.
Let's get lots of different shots of this cocoon."
Then some time passed.
Every day they kept filming the cocoon.
One day, the cocoon split open.{p}

A long beak, tentacles sprouting from its head, slimy, glistening eyes.
The creature that came out had turned into something grotesque.
But they remembered how it had been when it was little and so attached to them, and they pulled themselves together.
And they went back to filming.
From that day on, students at the school began to go missing, one after another.{p}

One time, they held a night shoot.
When they went to where the cocoon was, as usual, the creature wasn't there.
Tokita and the others searched the old school building.
And then, when they reached a classroom on the second floor...{p}

That thing, like a little red cherry-blossom seashell... was a human fingernail.
What it had been feeding on was a student from the class next to Tokita's.{p}

"Wh-whaaaaah☆"
Without thinking, they ran.
They could hear the creature coming after them.
Tokita ran blindly, shouting for help at the top of his lungs.{p}

Outside the old school building, beautiful moonlight lit up the surroundings.
He'd managed to get away.
Were the others all right?
But he didn't have the courage to go back and look for them.
"I-I'll go to the police..."
And just as he turned around...{p}

...That creature was right there.
The creature let out a sweet cry and thrust out its tentacles.
The tentacles dug into his body and released something inside it.
He felt a jolt as if something had burst inside him, and he passed out.{p}

...The next day, Tokita and the other members of the Film Research Society were found and taken to the hospital.
It seems they'd all been attacked by that creature.
They're still in the hospital even now.
Hm? The creature?
It's been missing since that night.
And no more students at the school have gone missing, either.
I don't know why Tokita and the others weren't eaten.
This is something I heard when I went to visit them, but apparently they've developed something like tumors in their brains.
And I hear the tumors are getting bigger day by day.
What on earth could they be?
But they're doing fine, I hear.
They seem to have healthy appetites, too.
Well, I intend to keep watching to see what happens to them from here on.
That's all I know.
Next person, please.{p}

Love and romance, is it?
So you're a romantic, {a}.
I hate anything that calls itself romance.
I believe a real man shouldn't lose himself in romance.
...Well, let's set that subject aside.
Actually, what I'll be telling you about this time is a comedy movie made at this school.{p}

Drama, is it?
...That's nice.
I'm rather fond of home dramas and that sort of thing.
I love ones that warm your heart, or ones with a happy ending.
But what I'll be telling you about this time has to do with a sci-fi movie.{p}

So you like comedy?
Then shall I tell you about a comedy movie made at this school?{p}

The one who planned that movie was a student named Tokita.
He was in the same class as me in first year.
Tokita was in the newspaper club, just like you, {a}.
And he was also a member of the film club.
He was aiming for a career in journalism, and he did both clubs for the sake of his future.
Back then there was a lot of bullying at this school, and he saw it as a real problem, so he set out to make a documentary.
"This issue deserves to be reported."
That's how fired up he was.
"The Reality of Bullying from a High Schooler's Point of View"
That's the kind of thing he was aiming for.{p}

Every day, he filmed the bullying with a hidden camera.
(This is awful...)
That's what he thought to himself.
But he never once stepped in to stop it.
I suppose he felt it would mean more to finish this footage and deal with the root of the problem than to fix just the tip of the iceberg.
He narrowed the documentary down to one particular bullied student.
From then on, he followed that student every single day.
But it's a strange thing. The bullying that had seemed so awful to him at first gradually became nothing more than a subject for his lens.{p}
Then one day, that student jumped off the roof and killed himself.

Tokita was filming it, of course.
They say that as the student fell, he noticed Tokita and looked sadly into the camera.{p}

How should he edit the footage he'd shot?
He thought it over.
Then he asked the members of the film society for help and decided to turn it into a comic film.
He would raise the problem through laughter. That was his idea.{p}

He started editing.
Editing is a kind of sorcery, isn't it?
With cheerful music, sound effects and the way the film is spliced together, grim footage of bullying turns into a comedy.
Though it also helped that the society members really knew what they were doing.{p}

The comedy was shown at the school festival.
The audience laughed a lot, you know.
Without knowing it was a tragedy that had really happened.
Maybe the truly frightening thing is the crowd, people like that.
As long as they think it's fiction, they can laugh at someone else's misery.
No, even if they knew it was true, they might still laugh.
I even got the feeling they would.{p}

After the film, the staff were introduced.
The audience applauded loudly.
"That was a wonderful comedy."
Tokita tried to say something to the emcee who'd said that.
This isn't just a comedy.
I suppose that's what he was feeling.
But his hesitant attempt was soon drowned out by the cheers of the audience.
I could read Tokita's feelings as clearly as if I held them in my hand.
If he told them the film's true meaning now, wouldn't it kill the mood?
Wouldn't the cheers turn into complaints...?
And so Tokita answered the audience's applause with a broad smile.
People's attitudes really do change in front of a crowd, don't they?{p}

After that, Tokita ended up making a second installment of the comedy.
Apparently the school was paying for the production, so he was trying to gather good equipment.
He seemed to be having the time of his life.
His only goal became making films that would go over well. Nothing else.{p}

Then one day, inexplicable accidents began to happen.
The friends who'd helped edit his film had accidents, one after another.
Besides them, plenty of other students had accidents too.
Traffic accidents, injuries in P.E. class... though none of them were life-threatening.
Tokita thought, could it be...?
He took out the staff notes from the school festival and the list of audience members, and checked the names.
"I knew it. The people whose names are written here are the ones having accidents."
At that point, it never even occurred to him that he himself was at the center of this film.{p}

Tokita picked up his video camera and set out to interview the victims.
Just then, he sensed something and turned around.{p}

"Y-you're..."
Standing there was the student who'd killed himself, the one he'd filmed for the first comedy.
Tokita sank to the floor in terror.
"What did you make that film for?"{p}

So said the student's ghost.
"And what kind of film are you making now?"
The pale-faced ghost reached out toward Tokita.
Tokita couldn't say a thing.
The spot between his eyes burned with fear, and tears welled up.
The ghost touched the video camera in Tokita's hand.
And then..................{p}

The next day, Tokita was found dead in the newspaper club's room.
This very club room, I mean.
It's better if I don't describe the body.
You might not be able to eat your dinner tonight.
I'll just say it was a pretty gruesome death.
Tokita's death must have been the grudge of the student who killed himself.
But why did he curse the people who showed the film and laughed at it, instead of the students who bullied him?
Grudges are strange things, aren't they?
Huh? How do I know this story, you ask?
After Tokita died, I found a videotape in this room, and on it, his interviews and his death were recorded with a comic touch.
There wasn't the slightest trace of sadness or fear in that footage.
{a}, you'd better not take your newspaper club work too far.
This seven wonders project of yours is material that won't stay just a joke, either.
That's the end of my story.
Next, please.{p}

...I see.
Once you get interested in the making side of films, you may not be able to simply enjoy watching them anymore.
That may differ from person to person, though...
So, let's say, hypothetically, you were going to work in film.
Well, it's only hypothetical, so just answer casually.
{a}, which one would you choose?{p}

I thought so.
{a}, you like to be in the spotlight, don't you?
Actors stand out more than anyone, after all. It's flashy, glamorous work.
And the actors are the ones who get popular, too.{p}

But it's hard work.
Because it's what people see, skill or the lack of it shows more than anywhere else.
The actors I think are amazing can handle any role flawlessly.
Well, that's how actors are supposed to be, of course.
...Tokita wanted to be the director.
Apparently that was settled without any fuss.{p}

A cameraman?
How faithfully can you capture what the director asks for, following the storyboards?
With what sensibility do you express the work through the camera?
When the director or the producer says it's no good, you reshoot it again and again...
I'd think you have to push your own opinions with the staff, yet still stay obedient.
When you think about it like that, it seems pretty difficult.
After all, if all it took was pointing the camera, anyone could do it.
Most people choose a film by its actors or director.
I won't say nobody goes to see a film because of who the cameraman is, but there can't be many.
It's not that he wanted to stand out, but Tokita wanted to be the director.
He'd wanted to direct for a long time, after all.
Apparently no one objected.{p}

That's the person who oversees everything: the money, the overall schedule, the image of the work, their own vision.
Of all these jobs... well, it's questionable whether you can even call it a job, but it's the one with the most say, isn't it?
If it were just putting up the production money and leaving the rest to everyone else, it would be easy, but grasping the whole thing and overseeing it must be tough.
Every one of these jobs is tough, though.
It's a work you're producing with your own money, so you can't do it halfway.
If the production drags on, you might be so anxious and worried that you never get a moment's peace.
It seems like a job full of worries.
Tokita wanted to be the director.
Apparently no one objected.{p}

A screenwriter?
That seems to call for writing skill.
On that point, {a}, as a reporter for the newspaper club, you seem used to writing.
Then there's the dialogue, building the story, meetings with the film's director, getting your ideas across...
But it sounds like hard work.
It seems you can't just write the script and say, 'There, the rest is up to you all...'
Well, that's obvious, of course.
Tokita wanted to be the director.
Apparently no one objected.{p}

My, that's a rather understated choice.
When we say 'the crew behind the scenes,' that covers sets, props and so on.
There seem to be even finer divisions, but I'll skip those this time.
As the name says, I think it's plain, grueling work where you never step out front yourselves.
But when something turns out unexpectedly well, better than you'd hoped, it must make you really happy.
They say many people in those jobs are very particular.
Whatever they do, they never forget their own standards...
In a sense, they're artists, I suppose.
I think that devotion is what makes the things they create all the better.
In the society, there wasn't really a proper crew for sets and props.
The members took care of it themselves, making things or bringing them from home.{p}

Tokita was the director.
It seems he'd wanted to direct for a long time.
He was also personally good at sculpting and modeling, so he seemed confident about props and makeup as well.
No one in particular objected to him directing.
And so the shooting of the society's memorable first production began.
I think it was right around this time last year.{p}

The film he set out to make was a horror movie titled 'The Mummy Man and the Beauty.'
...Who's that laughing?
Admittedly, it's a cheesy-sounding title.
But it's a shame to laugh like that.
Tokita was truly giving it everything he had.
He studied hard how to create the most effective scenes on a limited budget.
The guys who'd seemed eager at first gradually got bored, as they do.
In the end, they only did what they wanted to and wouldn't touch anything that didn't interest them or was hard work.
Most of them had joined half for fun, after all.{p}

A mummy brought over from Egypt comes back to life and searches for the reincarnation of the princess he once served.
In the end, he turns her into a mummy too, puts her in his coffin with him, and the two of them return to Egypt...
Since they were all amateurs, the shoot seems to have been rough.
Eventually, one way or another, the shooting was finished.{p}

But that's when the real trouble started.
You probably think a film is done once it's shot, but you'd be dead wrong.
Whether it turns out entertaining or not depends on the editing that comes next.
You take the scattered scenes on all the film you've shot and splice them together one by one.
And then a single film is complete.
Apparently it's work that takes a lot of patience.
Though for people who love it, I imagine it's irresistibly fun.
And Tokita was one of them, but...{p}

Somehow, once he started editing, it was quite different from what he'd imagined.
It's only something students shot, so expecting much was unreasonable to begin with.
But everything he'd thought was good while he was shooting it couldn't help looking like trash to him now.
"We'll have to reshoot it..."{p}

He told everyone in the society about it.
But they all objected. Redo it, at this point?
"It's just a movie some high schoolers made on their own, isn't it?
No matter how many times you shoot it, it'll come out the same.
Can't you even understand that?
With something like this, what matters is seeing it through, however it turns out."
So said the faculty advisor.
"We worked hard on it, and you call it trash? That kills anyone's motivation."
One of the members spat the words out.
Then, one by one, the ones who'd come to resent Tokita quit.
"This is why amateurs are...
Fine, anyone who wants to quit can go ahead and quit.
Only the ones who really mean it need to stay."
Saying that, Tokita didn't even try to stop them.{p}
Before long, they were finally down to just four people.{p}{a}, would you have stayed?
Stay in the society
Quit the society

You'd stay?
Well, I can understand that.
Tokita was a passionate person.
The ones who stayed in the society must have been moved by his passion too.
Wanting to finish the work with just those of them who were left...
I think Tokita had a kind of charisma.
That must be why they believed in him and stayed, even after he said something so outrageous.{p}

Among the members who stayed was Taichi Nakayama, who was in the same year as Tokita and me.
He was the one shooting the film with an 8mm camera.{p}

Tokita started the reshoot with the ones who were left.
He was careful not to repeat his earlier mistakes.
And he seemed obsessed with the makeup for when the mummy's bandages come off.
There was a scene like that.
He went through trial and error, trying it this way and that.
In the end, they left just that scene unshot and went ahead with the other scenes first.{p}

Then one day, Nakayama came down with a cold and was laid up for about four days.
During that time, Tokita did the filming.
He seemed fairly confident in his own camera skills, too.
Then Nakayama got over his cold, and it seems the shooting wrapped without a hitch.{p}

But just as they were about to start editing, Nakayama announced he was quitting the society.
The shooting was over, so that was enough, he said.
It seems he'd stayed in the society planning that from the start.{p}What do you think Tokita did?
He tried to make him stay
He told him he could quit

"You too... Why?
Please, I'm begging you, won't you at least help with the editing...?
There are things only you can do."
